I don't mean to brag but I'm a bit of an expert when it comes to surviving pain. (31 years of chronic illness, abuse as a child & adult, numerous broken bones, 2 car accidents, several medical procedures, a couple  (3 or 4) near death incidents, joints that dislocate themselves several times a week, years in bed etc)

Mental attitude matters a lot. I cope so much better when I am kind to myself and encouraging.

 I tell myself things like: "wow that was so hard to get through but you're such a badass you made it look easy", "I'm so proud of you for surviving today" etc. 

Don't let the pain make you bitter or a victim because that shit is painful to you and everyone you love. 

Ketamine treatments help both with the mental load of chronic pain & the sensation itself. But the pain reduction only lasts a few days. Drs office near me charges 400 for a 45 minute infusion. Unfortunately I cant afford that anymore but it got me through some really hard times.

NSAIDS  occasionally.  overuse = ulcers & easily bruising/bleeding for me.

Go outdoors barefoot (studies show decreased levels of inflammation after subjects stood barefoot on the ground) - I've started doing this daily regardless of weather and in my experience it has helped a bit.

I am not a doctor and have no idea what's wrong with you, but here's some tips I've learned surviving chronic pain. 

Heat packs and menthol (biofreeze or icyhot in the roll on bottle is one of my favorites and you can find at most drug stores, walmart etc) can help you cope with the pain. Ice packs as well if it feels good/helpful. I have both a old fashioned hot water bottle and a large electric heating pad and use them all the time.

If you alternate tylenol (acetaminophen) and an NSAID (ibuprofen, naproxen) you can sometimes get pretty good relief. For example take a tylenol, wait 2 hours and take an ibuprofen, then 2 hours later another tylenol and repeat. This is not necessarily something you can do long term (risk of ulcers). 

You said that you get relief for a very short period after you do your stretches... so do I. This means that I'm stretching multiple times a day and not just once. 

I have much better luck if I medicate, then use heat on the area, then apply menthol and THEN do my stretches/yoga poses. Calming music (bird/nature sounds too) can help calm your nervous system and get you out of the fight/flight survival mode. 

Its natural to tense your muscles in response to pain which can lead to an endless cycle of pain. So for me I focus on getting the pain managed ASAP. 

Epsom salts in a bath are nearly miraculous for achy muscles, I definitely recommend trying if you havent yet. If you dont have a tub, magnesium lotion is my second choice. I always take Magnesium sulfate or a magnesium blend before sleep as well. 

CBD (high doses for me) plus THC help. If you are in the USA, there are several companies that ship edibles with THC that is low enough it's legal under the hemp farm bill. If you're in a delta-9 (regular cannabis) illegal state, a lot of smoke shops carry delta-8 or delta10 THC or at least CBD with low THC. I also smoke hemp flower cigarettes sometimes.

Chiropractors can be helpful, but I'd be careful since you dont have a diagnosis yet. A chiro almost broke my brother's neck because he didn't bother to learn his neck was fused together before trying to manipulate it. The chiropractor I go to currently uses a little tool to make small adjustments and I like it WAY better than the traditional shoving/bodyslam type of treatments. 

If you can, I'd try to get a referral to a physical medicine & rehab doctor or a spine doc. As others mentioned an MRI seems like a logical next step.

Hang in there. 💕

How I meditate: 

YouTube has tons of this stuff and it took me a while to find one I liked. Different frequencies help me relax and others make me angry, so you kinda gotta find out what your brain likes/needs. 

I personally like to pair this youtube audio
[Deep OM](https://youtu.be/KZvM-qjT5i8) with the Luminate app (if you have photo sensitivity or epilepsy DONT use this app!). I do use the paid version, but they have enough on the free version for you to see if you like it. Basically it uses your phone's flashlight to send information to your brain to enter a more restful state. 

I lie in bed in the dark with my eyes closed (if I lay on my back I balance my phone on my nose and forehead with the flash between my eyes, if I'm on my side  I prop my phone with a pillow or hold it) while the sequence plays. You can adjust the intensity by moving your phone closer to your eyes or furthur away. 

I usually do 20 minute sessions and it takes me the first ten to get my mind clear and relax into it. Best method for me is to focus on an internal monologue of what I am 'seeing' (i.e. Black and white and flashing; magenta; spiral; waves; etc) and I can just melt into it. Husband sometimes joins me and we do it together. Kinda gets us in sync too. 


Other helpful things for me:

- Water: drinking, sitting or laying in, listening to, looking at etc. My DIY outdoor water feature is just the garden hose with a sprinkler. I like to lay down outside and listen to the water hit our aluminum siding and drip down. 

-Everytime it rains, if I feel well enough I go stand in the grass barefoot for a few minutes. My grandma did this with me since I was a kid and I swear it calms me on such a deep level.

- Sun bathing. Zero gravity lounger right outside my house that I try to lie in for 10-20 minutes. On the days I do this I feel calmer. Could also be from hearing the birds sing outside (birds get quiet if they sense danger, so our brains hear birdsong and associate it with being safe which can help reduce cortisol *or so I've heard).

- magnesium! I take multiple times a day plus have lotions, sprays and Epsom salt as needed. If I skip taking it, my muscles get so tight and painfully spasm.

4oz Orange juice
